Here's the full guide as a markdown doc you can keep. Quick summary of the key takeaways so you have them right here in chat:

What this is called: hybrid AI filmmaking / real-time hybrid filmmaking. Technically, V2V (video-to-video) restyling with character/environment replacement.

Your core stack should be:

Runway Aleph for stylizing your hero shots (5-sec clip limit is the main constraint to plan around)

Wan 2.2 Animate Replace for swapping stunt performers with demons — it preserves the original motion, expressions, and lighting via a built-in Relighting LoRA

Gen-4 References / Nano Banana Pro for locking your hero's stylized look once and reusing across shots

Beeble if you need to relight anything in post

Topaz Video AI + DaVinci Resolve for finishing

Three things to do before you touch a camera:

Build a 12–20 image style bible (hero + 4–6 demon designs + hallway moods)

Run a 10-second test plate through Aleph to see what works

Storyboard all 5 shots tightly — every second is going to cost AI credits

Shooting rules that matter most:

4K, 24fps, 1/48 shutter, log profile

Soft directional lighting, single color temp (you can change the mood in post)

Gimbal > handheld — smooth motion converts cleaner

Slow camera moves down ~15%

Wardrobe on stunt performers should match demon proportions and be fitted

Push performance ~10–15% bigger than realistic

Capture clean plates, grey ball, and HDRI on every setup

Best tutorial to watch first: Addy's "How To: Hybrid AI & Live Action Filmmaking Tutorial (Nano Banana Pro, Kling, Wan, Resolve)" on YouTube — it's the most current end-to-end walkthrough I found that matches your exact workflow. Yes — and they each solve a different problem in your film

I undersold these in the first guide. Both deserve a proper place in your stack. Here's the honest breakdown of what each one actually does, and where they fit your demon-hallway film.

Kling 3.0 Motion Control — your demon performance tool

This is the one that genuinely changes how you should think about your shoot. It's not video-to-video like Aleph. It's image-to-video driven by a motion reference:

You upload a character image (a demon design, in your case)

You upload a reference video (3–30 seconds) of a real performer doing the action

The model produces a video of your demon character performing the exact same motion — body movement, facial expression, hand gestures, camera rhythm, all transferred

What makes 3.0 different from 2.6 is "Element Binding" — it locks facial identity across the whole clip even through camera moves, occlusions, and turns. Kling 3.0 Motion Control extracts key facial information from uploaded images or videos and uses it as a reference to guide the generated animation, ensuring the character maintains the same identity, expressions, and visual clarity throughout the video.

Where this beats Wan 2.2 Animate Replace for your project: Wan replaces a character inside an existing video, preserving the original scene. Kling Motion Control regenerates the entire scene with your character in a new environment. So:

Use Wan Replace when you want to keep your hallway as-is and just swap the human stuntman with a demon. Same lighting, same background, same camera.

Use Kling Motion Control when you want the demon to appear in a fully different stylized environment (e.g. you shot the action in a plain warehouse but want the final demon to be in a hellscape). It pulls the motion choreography out of your performance and puts it onto a new character in a new world.

For an action sequence with multiple demon types, this is genuinely powerful. Shoot one stunt performer doing all the demon attacks. Then run the same plate through Kling MC with 4 different demon images → you get 4 different demon attacks with the same choreography. That's a level of creative iteration that wasn't possible a year ago.

Practical specs: Up to 30 seconds per generation (pick "video" orientation mode for the 30s cap; "image" mode caps at 10s). 1080p at "pro" mode, 720p at "std." Available via Replicate, Higgsfield, Artlist AI Toolkit, Media.io, or kling.ai directly.

Seedance 2.0 — your previz and inserts engine

Seedance is a different beast. It's text-to-video and image-to-video first, but with a multi-modal twist that makes it valuable in pre-production and for non-performance shots:

You can feed it up to 9 images, 3 video clips, 3 audio files, and a text prompt. The model understands how to use each piece. You can pull the composition from a photo, the camera movement from a video clip, the rhythm from an audio track, and describe how it all works together in words.

The killer feature for your project is timestamp-based prompting. You can direct individual shots within a single 15-second generation by writing timestamps into the prompt, like:

[0-4s]: wide establishing shot, static camera, dim hallway, character closes book
[4-9s]: medium shot, slow push-in, character stands and walks toward door
[9-15s]: close-up, low angle, character's hand on door handle

That's a complete 3-shot previz from a single generation. For a 5-shot film, you can previz the entire short in two Seedance calls before you ever touch a camera.

What Seedance is not great for: it doesn't do true V2V restyling like Aleph. If your output depends on a specific beat, hand position, or lens feel, the Seedance 2.0 reference video path is usually worth it. If you're exploring vibes, I'll stay with text until I know what I actually want to lock down. The video reference influences motion and camera, but the model is fundamentally generating new pixels rather than restyling yours. So it won't preserve your actor's exact face and performance the way Aleph or Wan will.

Where Seedance fits your film:

Previz the entire short before shooting (huge value, low cost)

Generate pure-AI inserts — wide reveals of the demon hallway, atmospheric establishing shots, the "all over" door at the end where there's no human performance to preserve

Generate the demon character reference images themselves (its image generation via Seedream 4.5 is excellent and your designs feed into Wan/Kling/Aleph)

Bridge shots — its video extension and fusion features can create 5-second transitions between your live-action shots when you need them

One thing I want to flag

The Kling vs Wan choice is genuinely the most important decision for your demon shots, and the right answer is probably both, on different shots. Wan preserves more (scene, lighting, original camera pixels) which is good for shots where the demon is interacting inside the real hallway. Kling regenerates more (whole scene from scratch with your demon design and your stuntman's motion) which is good for shots where you want stylization to dominate.

Test both on your same plate during your shoot day. Pick per-shot.

what should be my iphone 16 pro camera setting for shooting tmrw?

Good — shooting tomorrow means we're optimizing for what the AI tools downstream actually want. Here's your iPhone 16 Pro setup, dialed for hybrid AI filmmaking.

Use the Blackmagic Camera app, not the native one

This is the single most important call. The native Camera app on iPhone 16 Pro will fight you with auto-everything and aggressive computational processing (HDR fusion, Smart HDR, Deep Fusion, Photonic Engine) that bakes in decisions you can't undo. AI V2V models hate this — they prefer clean, flat, predictable footage.

Download Blackmagic Camera (free). It gives you full manual control, ProRes Log recording, and disables the computational layer. If you don't have it, second choice is the native app in ProRes Log mode (Settings → Camera → Formats → Apple ProRes + Pro Default to ProRes Log).

Core settings for tomorrow

Codec: Apple ProRes Log (or ProRes 422 HQ if you can't shoot Log)
Resolution: 4K (3840×2160)
Frame rate: 24 fps
Shutter: 1/48 sec (180° shutter angle — Blackmagic app shows this as "180°" in the angle setting)
ISO: Native ISO is 55 for low gain, 2500 for high gain on iPhone 16 Pro main camera. Stay at 55 if you have enough light. Don't go above 800 unless you have to — noise becomes AI flicker fuel.
White balance: Set manually. Don't use Auto. Pick the actual color temp of your dominant light source (3200K tungsten, 5600K daylight, etc). If unsure, shoot a white sheet of paper, lock to that.
Color profile: Apple Log (in Blackmagic app: Color Space → Apple Log; Gamma → Apple Log)
Aspect ratio: 16:9 for cinematic. If you might want vertical for social later, shoot 4K open-gate equivalent and crop in post.
Focus: Manual. Tap to set, then long-press to lock AE/AF. Auto-focus pulls during a take will create motion artifacts the AI exaggerates.
Stabilization: OFF. This is counter-intuitive but important — iPhone's optical/digital stabilization warps the frame edges subtly, and AI V2V notices. Use a gimbal for stabilization instead.

Storage — don't get caught short

ProRes Log at 4K/24 burns about 6 GB per minute. Plan accordingly:

A 256GB iPhone has maybe ~150GB free realistically → ~25 minutes of ProRes

Bring a USB-C SSD. iPhone 16 Pro records ProRes 4K directly to external SSD via USB-C. Any cheap 1TB Samsung T7 / SanDisk Extreme works. This is non-negotiable for a real shoot day.

USB-C cable must be a real USB 3 cable (the one in the box is USB 2 — too slow). Use the cable that came with a recent MacBook or a Thunderbolt cable.

Lens choice

iPhone 16 Pro has three cameras. Use them deliberately:

Main 24mm equivalent (f/1.78) — your default. Best sensor, shallowest depth of field, best low light. 90% of your shots.

Ultrawide 13mm (f/2.2) — only for very tight hallway wides. Distorts faces at close distance. AI tools handle the wide distortion fine but it can look cheap.

Telephoto 120mm (f/2.8, 5x optical) — for the close-up on your hand-on-the-door, the close-up on the demon's face. Compresses space nicely. Smaller sensor though, so needs more light.

Avoid the in-between digital zooms. 2x and 3x on iPhone are sensor crops + AI upscales — they look soft and confuse V2V models. Stick to native focal lengths (1x, 0.5x, 5x).

Lighting check before each take

Three things to verify on the iPhone screen:

Zebras at 95% (turn them on in Blackmagic settings). If zebras cover your subject's face, you're clipping highlights — pull back the exposure or add ND.

False color if you have it — keep faces in the green/pink zone, not red.

Histogram — your subject's tones should be sitting in the middle third, not bunched at either end.

If you're outside or in bright daylight, you'll need an ND filter for the iPhone (Moment makes a magnetic mount system, ~$60). Without it, you can't hit 1/48 shutter at f/1.78 in daylight without overexposing.

Audio

Don't bother trying to capture good production audio with the iPhone alone. The built-in mics are okay for reference scratch only. For your action piece you'll be doing full sound design in post anyway, so:

Record scratch audio on the phone (it auto-records)

If you want better scratch, plug in a Rode VideoMic Me-C or similar via USB-C

Have someone clap at the start of each take for sync

Two things specific to your AI workflow

Shoot a test clip first thing. Before any "real" takes, shoot 10 seconds of your actor in the hallway with these settings. Run it through Aleph as soon as you can (even later that day). If something is wrong with your settings, you find out before you've shot the whole film.

Shoot reference plates at every setup:

5 seconds of empty hallway (clean plate)

5 seconds of someone holding a grey card or white sheet of paper at the actor's position (lighting reference)

360° pan of the location (rough HDRI for Beeble/relight later)

These take 30 seconds each and save you days in post.

The settings cheat sheet for tomorrow

App: Blackmagic Camera
Codec: Apple ProRes Log
Resolution: 4K 16:9
Frame rate: 24 fps
Shutter angle: 180° (= 1/48 sec)
ISO: 55 (or 2500 if very low light)
White balance: Manual, set to source
Focus: Manual, locked
Stabilization: OFF
Lens: 1x main / 5x telephoto for close-ups
Storage: External USB-C SSD
ND filter: if shooting daylight

One last thing — charge your phone fully tonight and bring a power bank. ProRes recording + screen on + gimbal control will kill an iPhone battery in about 90 minutes of active shooting.

Good luck tomorrow. Send me a test clip after the shoot and I can help you assess whether it'll work for Aleph before you commit to your full edit.

Tap "SHUTTER," disable Auto, set to 180° angle (or 1/48 if you didn't change Shutter Measurement yet). 1/33 is a weird in-between value the auto picked — it'll create motion artifacts.

ISO: 858 (Auto) ❌ → set manually to 55 if lit, or 2500 if dark
iPhone 16 Pro main camera has dual native ISO at 55 and 2500. Anything between those values is worse than either base ISO because it's gained up from 55. ISO 858 is in the noisy middle zone. Always pick one of the two natives:

Bright / well-lit hallway → ISO 55

Dim hallway, no extra light → ISO 2500

Don't sit between them

WB: 4950K (Auto) ❌ → lock manually
Tap WB, disable Auto, set to whatever your dominant light source is:

Tungsten / warm practicals: 3200K

Mixed / unknown indoor: 4000K

Daylight / window light: 5600K

LED panels: check the panel's spec (usually 5600K)

Then once locked, don't change it during the shoot day unless lighting fundamentally changes.

TINT: -12 — leave this alone unless you see a clear green or magenta cast in the picture.

LENS: 24mm ✓ — your default. Stay here for 90% of shots.

FPS: 24 ✓ — perfect.

EXPOSURE COMPENSATION (the +/- A icon) — turn this off Auto too. With manual ISO + manual shutter, you're fully manual.

FOCUS (the [O] A icon on the right) — turn off Auto. Tap to set focus on your subject's eye, then lock. Auto-focus pulls during a take create artifacts AI hates.

The "ready to shoot" state

When you're set up correctly, the bottom bar should show:

LENS: 24mm
FPS: 24
SHUTTER: 180°  (no blue "A" badge)
IRIS: f1.78    (fixed, can't change on iPhone)
ISO: 55        (no blue "A" badge)
WB: [your value]K  (no blue "A" badge)

No blue "A" badges anywhere. If you see an A, that setting is still on auto and will drift.

Two extra things to enable before tomorrow

In the Camera tab on the live view, tap the three dots and look for:

Zebras at 95% — turn on. Tells you when highlights clip. If zebras cover your actor's face → reduce exposure.

Focus Peaking — turn on. Shows you what's sharply in focus. Critical when you're locked manual focus.

Some versions of Blackmagic Camera also have False Color — if available, turn it on. Skin tones should sit in the green/pink range.

Quick action list before you walk out the door tomorrow

☐ Plug in external SSD, verify it's recording to it (not internal)

☐ Set Bit Rate to Max

☐ Turn HDR Video OFF

☐ Switch Shutter Measurement to Angle

☐ On the camera screen: disable all the "A" auto badges (Shutter, ISO, WB, Exposure, Focus)

☐ Set Shutter to 180°

☐ Set ISO to 55 (bright) or 2500 (dim) — never between

☐ Set WB manually based on your hallway lights

☐ Enable Zebras at 95% and Focus Peaking
